messages.body_plain:
Toby and I as co-admins (backups are Virgilio and Brian to ensure depth) have had a phone
conversation and would like to put forward some policies based on experiences in previous
years (these are reported in the article by Claudia Beleites and I at
http://journal.r-project.org/archive/2011-2/RJournal_2011-2.pdf).

In particular, we suggest that R only put forward for funding projects that:

- have at least 2 mentors -- one student last year was left without contact for a while
and the admins could not contact the mentor either. We think that an idea that cannot get
two people to offer to mentor it does not have sufficient interest.

- have a student who has given at least 2 methods of communication -- channels do get broken

- have a plan for student/mentor communication (Google more or less asks for this too)

Are there other ideas that deserve to be in place? We don't want to make this onerous, but
more to suggest factors that will enhance the success of R's participation in GSOC.

Best,

John Nash

messages.subject: Project idea - wikipediaR
messages.body_plain:
Hello everyone,

I have a project idea.
There is no package for Wikipedia articles. That surprised me, because one could do a lot of interesting statistical analysis with Wikipedia's content,  for example do text mining on the articles using the tm package or analyze the backlinks, plot wordclouds and so on.

The package should contain a function which provides a convenient way for retrieving whole Wikipedia articles. The user puts the topics as strings in and gets the articles as output.
This could happen via different sources. One would be online using the official Wikipedia API (http://en.wikipedia.org/w/api.php).
This source would need the RCurl and XML package.
Another source could be the Wikipedia xml dump files. They contain all of the articles which results in pretty huge files (2.5GB). I think one does not want to use R for parsing such an amount of data. The solution could be to use an external program or import the dump into a SQL table and read it with R using the RMySQL package.

An article could be stored as a S4-object. Other formats like S3 or a simple list would also be possible.

The package should in addition provide some functions for preparing the articles for text mining and other statistical analysis.
I would also add some functions for a first explorative analysis, like summary and plot methods.

What do possible mentors think about this project idea? Is this interesting enough for the R community?
I'm also interested in the image labels project.
It would be great to hear your thoughts about my proposal, so that I can decide on which to focus on.

If you like the project idea, do you want to be my mentor?

Best regards
Christoph Molnar

On 12-03-26 09:08 PM, Carl Boettiger wrote:
> Hi John,
>
> I'm one of the mentors with the rOpenSci project.  We're new to GSoC, and I think I've
> grasped the basic idea about how this works but I have a few questions I'd like to run by
> you.
>
> At this point we've had a few different students contact us and express interest.  I
> understand that in the next stage, the R-GSoC project will be awarded funds for some
> number /n /students and the organizers (you and Toby?) will then decide how to allocate
> these resources to mentor/student pairs?

Actually, we ask all the mentors to comment and rank all the projects they feel competent
to judge (and to hopefully leave alone those out of their domain of expertise). Then the
admins check the proposals:
     - do they have basic requirements of >1 mentor, contact info, communication plan etc.
     - has the student shown competence (i.e., completed test or shown work or ....)

Then we look at rankings -- this is where it gets tough. If we are lucky, then there are
clear rankings. BUT -- sometimes two very good projects for one topic and none for
another. The admins generally act like chairpersons -- they break ties. But sometimes we
have to make some suggestions and try to bring in externalities e.g., benefits to R as a
whole. But in my experience we try to reflect the consensus and diligently avoid our own bias.

Melange shows the rankings to Google who declare the number of slots we have, and we then
have to make a final selection. Sometimes a student gets a "real" job. That has happened
and fortunately in time to reassign the slot.

>
> I'm a bit fuzzy as to the best practices for this selection process.  For instance, at
> this time, should we be trying to identify a best student candidate from among those
> interested, or can we put forward multiple students that have proposed to work with some
> aspect of rOpenSci?  In the later case, I assume we would still be awarded at most 1
> student?  Should we be asking interested applicants for CVs or anything formal at this
> stage?  Or will that material all be part of the student's applications on the 6th?  Are
> we involved in the student ranking/scoring process or does that refer to your selection
> process?
>
The students should be encouraged to put forward STRONG proposals
   - serious but short CV
   - demonstration of competence and knowledge sufficient to complete project
   - good work plan with enough slack to cover "glitches"
   - documentation plan
   - communications plan
   - dissemination plan for results

I don't think project mentors should inhibit submissions. It is a competition, and we want
the best. Last year two good projects on one topic divided and did different aspects. That
is probably a good idea, as I think there is a general view that 2 on one topic is unfair
to other ideas.

Mentors can and should consider interpersonal skills. That is important in getting
projects to completion.

Hope this helps.

JN

If you can't easily locate the mentor for the projects you're looking
at, then feel free to post initial inquiries here, as you've done.  All
R project mentors should be on this list.

> Some ideas provide a TEST, should I complete it before application?
> and how can I interact with those mentors? Most ideas don't have an
> contact info so I don't know how to interact with these mentors to
> discuss about their project.

After initial email/irc/IM conversations with the project mentor, I
recommend that all students start on your applications ASAP. The
application process opened at the beginning of this week, and
applications may be modified until April 06 at 19:00 UTC on Google's
deadline.

It is possible for students to apply to more than one project, though
this is generally something we discourage.  We've found that students
who apply to multiple projects generally don't/can't take the time to do
a really good application.

My advice would be to communicate with potential mentor(s), pick one,
and work to craft the best possible application by the deadline.  The
sooner you post a draft application, the sooner you can get additional
feedback from other R mentors as well.
